title: Conditionals
summary: The four conditional patterns, mixed conditionals, alternatives to if, and inverted forms such as Had I known.

sections.heading: Zero and first conditionals: real situations
sections.body:
The **zero conditional** (`if` + present simple, present simple) states something that is always true: a law of nature, a rule, a machine's behaviour. `If` can usually be replaced by `when` without changing the meaning, which is a reliable test.

The **first conditional** (`if` + present simple, `will` + infinitive) treats a future event as a real possibility. The condition clause takes a present tense even though it refers to the future, exactly as after `when` and `as soon as`. `Will` in the if-clause is one of the commonest errors at this level.

examples.right: If the sensor records a temperature above forty degrees, the system shuts down.
examples.note: A rule that holds every time: zero conditional, present in both clauses.

examples.right: If the funding falls through, the department will have to cut two courses.
examples.wrong: If the funding will fall through, the department will have to cut two courses.
examples.note: The if-clause of a first conditional takes the present simple, never will.

examples.right: If you submit the form late, it may not be considered.
examples.note: The result clause can take may, might, can, should or an imperative instead of will.

sections.heading: The second conditional: unlikely or unreal now
sections.body:
`If` + past simple, `would` + infinitive presents a present or future situation as hypothetical, improbable or contrary to fact. The past tense here carries no past meaning at all; it is a marker of distance from reality.

The contrast with the first conditional is a matter of the speaker's commitment. `If it rains, we'll move indoors` treats rain as a live possibility; `If it rained in July, the reservoirs would recover` treats it as unlikely. With the verb `be`, `were` is standard for every person in careful writing, and `If I were you` is fixed.

examples.right: If the government subsidised rail travel, far fewer people would drive to work.
examples.note: A hypothetical policy and its imagined consequence.

examples.right: If I were you, I would apply before the deadline.
examples.wrong: If I would be you, I would apply before the deadline.
examples.note: Would never appears in the if-clause of a second conditional.

examples.right: If she took the post in Geneva, she would have to learn French.
examples.note: The past simple marks the offer as one she is not expected to accept.

sections.heading: The third conditional: an unreal past
sections.body:
`If` + past perfect, `would have` + past participle imagines a past that did not happen, and is the natural language of regret, blame and hindsight. Both clauses refer to past time, and both are counterfactual: the sentence asserts that neither event occurred.

The result clause can take `could have` or `might have` where the outcome is possible rather than certain. What it cannot take is the shape `if I would have`, which spreads from spoken American English but is not accepted in academic writing; the if-clause needs the past perfect and nothing else.

examples.right: If the committee had heeded the March warning, the outbreak could have been contained.
examples.wrong: If the committee would have heeded the March warning, the outbreak could have been contained.
examples.note: The if-clause of a third conditional takes the past perfect; would belongs only in the result.

examples.right: If I had known about the delay, I would not have booked the connecting flight.
examples.note: Both halves are contrary to fact: the delay was unknown and the flight was booked.

examples.right: The paper might have been accepted if the data had been checked more carefully.
examples.note: might have softens the claim; the tense pattern is unchanged when the clauses are reversed.

sections.heading: Mixed conditionals
sections.body:
The two halves of a conditional need not refer to the same time. A **past condition with a present result** combines `if` + past perfect with `would` + infinitive: something that did not happen in the past explains a state of affairs now.

The reverse, a **present condition with a past result**, combines `if` + past simple with `would have` + past participle: a permanent characteristic or present fact explains something that did or did not happen earlier. Choose each half for its own time reference rather than copying the pattern of the other.

examples.right: If she had won that scholarship, she would be studying in Berlin now.
examples.wrong: If she had won that scholarship, she would have been studying in Berlin now.
examples.note: Past cause, present result: the result clause takes would plus a bare infinitive.

examples.right: If he weren't so cautious, he would have accepted that offer years ago.
examples.note: A lasting present trait explaining a past decision.

examples.right: If the line had been built in the 1970s, the city would look very different today.
examples.note: The adverbials today and now are the usual signal of a mixed pattern.

sections.heading: Alternatives to if
sections.body:
**`unless`** means roughly `if not` and introduces the one circumstance that would prevent the result: `The council will refuse permission unless the developer funds the road`. It does not work for every negative condition, and it is never followed by a second negative.

**`provided that`** and **`as long as`** state a condition that must be satisfied, with more emphasis than `if`. **`in case`** is different in kind: it introduces a precaution taken in advance, not a condition, so `Take a map in case you lose signal` means take it now, before anything happens. **`even if`** concedes that the condition will not change the outcome, and **`otherwise`** replaces a whole negative clause: `Submit it by Friday; otherwise it will not be read`.

examples.right: The trial will continue unless the safety board intervenes.
examples.wrong: The trial will continue unless the safety board doesn't intervene.
examples.note: Unless already contains the negative; a second one reverses the meaning.

examples.right: Take the printed map in case your phone loses signal in the valley.
examples.wrong: Take the printed map if your phone loses signal in the valley.
examples.note: In case is a precaution taken beforehand; if would mean taking the map only after the signal is lost.

examples.right: The grant is renewable as long as the team publishes annually.
examples.note: As long as and provided that both state a requirement, and both take a present tense.

examples.right: Even if the appeal succeeds, the site will not reopen this year.
examples.note: Even if concedes the condition and denies it any effect.

sections.heading: Inversion and punctuation
sections.body:
In formal writing `if` may be dropped and the auxiliary moved in front of the subject: `Had I known`, `Were it not for the volunteers`, `Should you need further details`. Only `had`, `were` and `should` invert in this way, the negative is never contracted (`Had it not been for`, not `Hadn't it been for`), and the register is noticeably formal.

Punctuation follows position, not meaning. A conditional clause placed first is followed by a comma; when it comes second, no comma is used. This holds for every conditional type and for the inverted forms as well.

examples.right: Had I known about the funding cut, I would have submitted the proposal earlier.
examples.wrong: Had I known about the funding cut I would have submitted the proposal earlier.
examples.note: A fronted conditional clause takes a comma; the inverted form is the third conditional without if.

examples.right: Were it not for the volunteers, the project would have collapsed.
examples.wrong: Was it not for the volunteers, the project would have collapsed.
examples.note: The inverted form uses were for all subjects.

examples.right: Should you need further details, please contact the registry.
examples.note: Should here means if by any chance, and is common in formal correspondence.

examples.right: The project would have collapsed were it not for the volunteers.
examples.note: No comma when the conditional clause follows the main clause.

slips: No will in the if-clause of a first conditional: If it rains, we'll postpone, never If it will rain.
No would in the if-clause of a second or third conditional: If I had known, not If I would have known.
unless already means if not, so unless she doesn't apply says the opposite of what is intended.
in case is a precaution, not a condition: Insure the equipment in case it is stolen means insure it now, whereas if it is stolen refers to what happens afterwards.
In a mixed past-to-present conditional the result clause is would plus infinitive, not would have: she would be studying in Berlin now, not she would have been studying now.
Comma placement follows position: If the data are wrong, the model fails, but The model fails if the data are wrong.

questions.prompt: If the sensor ___ a temperature above forty degrees, the system shuts down automatically.
questions.explain: The present simple in the result clause marks this as a zero conditional describing an invariable rule, so the if-clause must also be present simple.

questions.prompt: If the committee ___ the warning issued in March, the outbreak could have been contained.
questions.explain: A third conditional pairs the past perfect in the if-clause with could have or would have in the result; would have heeded is the classic error.

questions.prompt: If I ___ you, I would apply for the grant well before the deadline.
questions.explain: Second conditionals distance the situation with a past form, and were is fixed in this advice-giving formula. would be can never stand in an if-clause.

questions.prompt: ___ I known about the funding cut, I would have submitted the proposal a month earlier.
questions.explain: This is a third conditional with if omitted and the auxiliary inverted. If I known is not English; the uninverted version would need If I had known.

questions.prompt: If she ___ that scholarship, she would be studying in Berlin now.
questions.explain: A mixed conditional: the past perfect states the unreal past cause, while would be studying keeps the result in the present.

questions.prompt: The council will refuse permission ___ the developer agrees to fund the new access road; if the money is offered, the scheme will go ahead.
questions.explain: The second half shows that agreement would reverse the refusal, which is exactly the if not meaning of unless. even if would deny the funding any effect, contradicting the sentence.

questions.prompt: Submit the application by Friday; ___ it will not be considered.
questions.hint: one word replacing 'if you do not'
questions.explain: Otherwise stands in for a whole negative conditional clause and needs no if of its own.

questions.prompt: Take the printed map with you ___ your phone loses signal in the valley.
questions.explain: In case introduces a precaution taken in advance. If would instruct the walker to take the map only once the signal had already gone, which is impossible.

questions.prompt: ___ not for the generosity of the volunteers, the project would have collapsed last year.
questions.hint: the inverted form of 'if it were not for' (two words)
questions.explain: Inversion replaces if with the fronted auxiliary, and were is used for all subjects in this formal pattern.

questions.prompt: If he weren't so cautious by nature, he ___ that offer years ago.
questions.explain: A permanent present trait explains a past non-event, so the result clause is would have plus a past participle. would accept would move the result into the present, clashing with years ago.

questions.prompt: If the government subsidised rail travel more heavily, far fewer people ___ to work.
questions.explain: The past simple in the if-clause signals a hypothesis, and the matching result form is would plus the bare infinitive.

questions.prompt: If the funding ___, the department will have to withdraw two courses next year.
questions.explain: A first conditional keeps the future meaning in the main clause only; the if-clause takes the present simple. fell through would turn a real risk into a remote hypothesis and would then require would in the result.
